newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH CENTRAL BANK MOVES TO SUPPORT CROWN AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: CZECH CENTRAL BANK MOVES TO SUPPORT CROWN AGAIN.

text.p: The Czech National Bank (CNB) moved again on Tuesday to shore up a shaky currency, sending commercial interest rates through the roof.
The central bank said it had begun to impose limits on banks' access to the last resort lending facility, the Lombard rate, to an unspecified portion of a bank's capital.

Last Friday the CNB raised the Lombard rate from 14 percent to 50 percent in a move aimed against speculative selling of the crown, once regarded as the most stable currency in post-communist central Europe.
One of the Czech Republic's leading banks, state-owned Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka a.s., reacted to the CNB's move on Tuesday by raising its prime rate to 25.00 percent from 11.75 percent.
CNB spokesman Martin Svehla told Reuters the central bank restriction applied equally to all foreign and Czech banks with a licence to operate in the country.
"We intend only to regulate somehow the access to the Lombard credit, and the intention is for equal (access) to the Lombard (based on) the capital of a bank," Svehla said.
"I deny that we are making any kind of difference between foreign and domestic banks ... Our treatment is the same -- the Lombard credit can be given adequately to a portion of capital," he added.
But Stefan Balgavy of German-owned Commerzbank said his bank, which operates as a licensed branch in Prague, was denied access to the lending facility outright.
This was because a branch's capital is small locally, and is calculated instead through its parent bank. Commerzbank is one of Germany's big three banks.
"I don't understand where they are going with this. It appears as though banks are not being treated equally," he said.
On Friday, the CNB said after raising the Lombard rate that it would, if necessary, restrict access to the Lombard facility altogether.

"Normally the Lombard rate is not used, but because banks are spending domestic currency and buying foreign currency, there could be a liquidity shortage," CNB board member Ludek Niedermeyer said on Friday.
"In such a circumstance, the central bank is not very happy to provide financing of speculation against the domestic currency."
The Czech crown has been heavily pressured over the past week as mainly foreign investors pushed the currency lower through short-selling.

The currency hit a record weak point of more than five percent below the midpoint of a dollar/mark basket which the CNB uses to fix the crown's exchange rate daily. This prompted the CNB to intervene in the market for the first time in over a year.
The CNB also allowed market conditions to determine its repurchase rate, which on Monday and Tuesday hit 45 percent after 12.9 percent on Friday.
The Czech Republic under economist Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus used to be praised in the West as a model for post-communist reform.
While the CNB has kept inflation in single figures, a soaring current account deficit raised concerns about the Czech economy and the government has slashed earlier forecasts of robust GDP growth.
The crown jumped about 40 basis points against the basket midpoint after CSOB raised its rates on Tuesday.
It was at 30.241 to the dollar and 17.833 to the mark, implying a deviation from basket midpoint of -1.63 percent, after trading at about -2.10 percent before the announcement.
"This is a clear signal that they (CSOB) will be takers of crowns, and has pushed the currency higher," said one London-based dealer.
-- Prague Newsroom, 420-2-2423-0003
